items.title: What the strategy may see
items.prose: A backtest engine loops over the bars one at a time. It has just reached the close of bar 4. The strategy compares the close with its 3-bar mean, a trailing window that ends at the current bar. Orders go out for the next open.
items.question: Tap every row the 3-bar mean uses at this close.

feedback.correct: Bars 2, 3 and 4: the last three closes known at the close of bar 4.
feedback.generic: The window ends at the current bar and reaches back three bars. Which three have closed?

byKey.r0: Bar 1 is four bars back, outside a 3-bar window.
byKey.r1: Bar 2 is the oldest of the last three closes. It is in the window.
byKey.r3: Bar 4 has just closed, so its close is known. The window ends there.
byKey.r4: Bar 5 has not started. Its prices do not exist at the close of bar 4.
byKey.r5: Bar 6 is two bars in the future.
byKey.lagged: You left out bar 4. Its close is known now, so the window ends there.
byKey.centred: You centred the window on bar 4. Bar 5 has not happened yet, so that window peeks.
byKey.history: That is the whole history. The 3-bar mean reads only the last three bars.

explain.text: At the close of bar 4 the last three closes are those of bars 2, 3 and 4. Their mean is (52.90 + 52.55 + 52.00) / 3 = 52.48. A centred window would need bar 5, which is still in the future.

items.title: Who is in the universe on 15 June 2021
items.prose:
A share is in the universe on a date if it passes three tests:

- it is listed on the date
- it has a full 60 days of history
- its 60-day mean £ volume is at least £5m

The file gives that mean to two dates. We may use only what was known on 15 June 2021. "none" means no figure exists.
items.question: Tap every share in the universe on 15 June 2021.

feedback.correct: AAA, EEE and FFF pass all three tests on that date.
feedback.generic: Test each share with the 15 June column only: listed, 60 days old and at least £5m.

byKey.survivors: You dropped EEE because it dies in November. On 15 June it is listed and liquid, so it belongs.
byKey.r0: AAA is listed, old enough and liquid. Keep it.
byKey.r1: BBB's last day was 3 March 2021. It is gone by 15 June.
byKey.r2: CCC's £4.6m to 15 June is under the £5m floor. Its later £8.0m was not known yet.
byKey.r3: DDD lists in August. A universe built on 15 June cannot know it.
byKey.r4: EEE dies in November, but on 15 June it is listed and liquid. A point-in-time universe keeps it.
byKey.r5: FFF's £5.0m to 15 June meets 'at least £5m'. Its later fall does not count yet.
byKey.r6: GGG listed on 4 May, about 30 trading days ago. It has no 60-day figure on 15 June.
byKey.year-end: You used the 31 December figures. On 15 June nobody knew them.

explain.text: AAA, EEE and FFF pass on the 15 June figures. BBB has died, DDD has not listed, CCC is too thin and GGG is too new. The December column would swap CCC, DDD and GGG in for EEE and FFF, which nobody could know in June.

items.title: Quotes the cleaner removes
items.prose:
One-month calls on a £100 share, snapshotted at 14:30. The cleaner keeps a quote only if all four hold:

- the bid is above 0
- the bid is not above the ask
- the quote is at most 30 minutes old
- (ask − bid) / mid is under 0.5
items.question: Tap every quote the cleaner removes.

feedback.correct: Four quotes fail a rule: stale, zero bid, crossed and too wide.
feedback.generic: Work out each quote's age from 14:30 first. Then check the four rules in turn.

byKey.r0: The £90 quote is from 12:55, 95 minutes before the snapshot.
byKey.r1: The £95 quote is fresh, and its spread of 0.30 on a mid of 5.95 is only 5%. It stays.
byKey.r2: The £100 quote is exactly 30 minutes old and passes the other three rules. It stays.
byKey.r3: A zero bid fails the first rule, however small the ask.
byKey.r4: The bid of 0.30 is above the ask of 0.20, so the quote is crossed.
byKey.r5: The spread of 0.08 equals the mid of 0.08, a ratio of 1.0. That is too wide.
byKey.r6: Spread 0.04 on a mid of 0.12 is 33%, under 0.5. Cheap is not wide.
byKey.edge: The £100 quote is exactly 30 minutes old. 'At most 30 minutes' keeps it.

explain.text: £90 is 95 minutes old, £105 has no bid and £110 is crossed. £115's spread equals its mid. £100 is exactly 30 minutes old and £120's spread is a third of its mid, so both stay.

items.title: The cost of one fill
items.prose: The engine buys 3,000 shares at £42.50, sent as 20 child orders of 150 shares each. Commission is £0.005 a share with a £1 minimum on each order. The half spread is 2 basis points of the traded value.
items.question: What do the 20 fills cost in total, in £?

feedback.correct: Each child pays the £1 minimum, £20.00 in all, plus £25.50 of half spread.
feedback.generic: Find one child's commission and apply the minimum. Then add 2 bp of the whole traded value.

byKey.one-order: You charged commission on one order of 3,000 shares. Each child order pays at least £1.
byKey.spread-only: You charged the spread but not the commission. The engine charges both.
byKey.commission-only: You charged the commission but not the half spread. Crossing the spread costs real money.
byKey.full-spread: You charged the whole spread, 4 bp. A fill pays half of it, 2 bp.

explain.text: Each child's commission is 150 × £0.005 = £0.75, below the minimum, so each pays £1.00: £20.00 in all. The half spread is 2 bp of £127,500, or £25.50, however the order is split. The total is £45.50, £5.00 more than one order of 3,000.

items.title: Twelve-minus-one on monthly returns
items.prose: Monthly log returns of one share, in percent, to the end of December. Build its 12-minus-1 momentum signal at the end of December.
items.question: What is the 12-minus-1 signal, in percent?

feedback.correct: January to November sum to 15%.
feedback.generic: Add the monthly returns from January to November. December is the month we skip.

byKey.all-twelve: You added December's −5 as well. The skip month is left out on purpose.
byKey.latest-only: −5 is December alone, the month that reverses. The signal is the other eleven.
byKey.dropped-oldest: You dropped January and kept December. The skip removes the latest month, not the oldest.

explain.text: The first eleven months sum to 15. December's −5 is skipped, because one-month returns tend to reverse.

items.title: One Newton step
items.prose: We solve for the implied volatility of a one-year at-the-money call by Newton's method. The share is £100, the strike £100, $r = 5\%$, no dividend. The market mid is £13.00. At $\sigma = 25\%$ the model price is £12.34. The risk system reports vega as 0.378 per volatility point.
items.question: Take one Newton step from 25%. What is the new volatility, in percent?

feedback.correct: The model is £0.66 too cheap, and 0.66 / 0.378 = 1.75 points.
feedback.generic: Newton's step is the price gap over vega. Mind the units: this vega is per volatility point.

byKey.minus: You moved volatility down. The model price is below the market, so volatility has to go up.
byKey.no-vega: You added the price gap straight to volatility. Divide by vega first.
byKey.per-unit: You read vega as per 1.00 of volatility. It is per point, so the step is 1.75 points.

explain.text: The gap is 13.00 − 12.34 = 0.66. With vega 0.378 per point, the step is 0.66 / 0.378 = 1.75 points. The new volatility is 26.75%, and the true implied volatility is also 26.75%.

items.title: One bar of the engine loop
items.prose: Orders fill at the next open. The engine keeps one order waiting from the previous bar. Five of these steps belong to one bar of the loop, in a shuffled order. Two do not.
items.question: Put the five steps in order and leave out the two that do not belong.

lines.text: Fill the order left over from yesterday, at today's open
Mark equity: cash plus shares at today's close
Give the strategy the history up to today's close
Turn the strategy's signal into a target position
Turn the change in target into an order for tomorrow's open
Fill the new order at today's close, the price the signal used
lines.why: That is a same-bar fill. The new order waits for tomorrow's open.

lines.text: Compute the signal once on the whole price file, before the loop
lines.why: A signal built on the whole file can read later bars. The loop hands over history one bar at a time.

feedback.correct: Fill at the open, then the close of the bar can be used, then the decision, then the order.
feedback.generic: Work out what each step needs. The fill needs yesterday's order. The new order needs the target, and the target needs the signal.

byKey.s1: Yesterday's order fills first, at the open. Nothing from today's close is known yet.
byKey.s2: Equity is marked at the close, after the fill has changed cash and shares.
byKey.s3: The strategy sees today's close only after the bar has ended, so after the open fill.
byKey.s4: The target comes from the signal, so the signal step must run first.
byKey.s5: The order is the last step. It needs the target, which needs the signal.

explain.text: The old order fills at today's open, before anything about today's close exists. Marking equity and handing over the history both wait for the close. Signal, target and order follow, and the order waits for tomorrow's open.

items.title: A split, then a dividend
items.prose: A share closes Monday at £240.00. On Tuesday it splits two-for-one and closes at £121.50. On Wednesday it pays £1.50 per share and closes at £122.00.
items.question: What is the total return from Monday's close to Wednesday's, in percent?

feedback.correct: One Monday share is two shares by Wednesday, each worth £122.00 plus £1.50 in cash.
feedback.generic: Follow one Monday share to Wednesday: two shares, their close and their dividends, against £240.00.

byKey.raw: You compared raw closes. The split halved the price, but the holder owns twice as many shares.
byKey.no-dividend: You adjusted for the split but left out the dividend. Each of the two shares received £1.50.
byKey.dividend-old: You paid the dividend once per old share. It is paid on each of the two new shares.

explain.text: One Monday share becomes two on Tuesday, and each pays £1.50 on Wednesday. The holding is worth 2 × (122.00 + 1.50) = £247.00. Against £240.00 that is 7 / 240 = 2.92%.

items.title: The dividend yield in an option pair
items.prose: From a six-month chain, the pair at strike £95: call mid £8.50, put mid £2.80. The share is £100 and the rate is 5% a year, continuously compounded.
items.question: What dividend yield $q$ do the two quotes imply, in percent?

feedback.correct: Parity gives a forward of £100.84, and $q = r - \ln(F/S)/T = 3.32\%$.
feedback.generic: Parity gives the forward: $F = K + e^{rT}(C - P)$. Then $F = S e^{(r-q)T}$ gives $q$.

byKey.no-T: You left out the division by T. Over half a year, $\ln(F/S)$ is half the yearly rate, so double it.
byKey.no-discount: You added C − P to the strike without the factor $e^{rT}$. The gap is paid at expiry, so it grows at the rate.
byKey.strike-as-spot: You divided the forward by the strike. The forward grows from the share price, £100.

explain.text: The forward is $F = 95 + e^{0.025} \times 5.70$, or £100.84. Then $q = 0.05 - \ln(1.00844)/0.5 = 0.05 - 0.0168 = 3.32\%$. Away from the money, both the strike and the time to expiry matter.

items.title: Doubling the order
items.prose: Impact per £ traded is $c\,\sigma\sqrt{Q/V}$, with $c = 1$, $\sigma = 1.5\%$ a day and daily volume $V = 1{,}600{,}000$ shares. Buying 40,000 shares at £60 costs £5,692.10 in impact. We now buy 80,000 shares at the same price.
items.question: What does the 80,000-share order cost in impact, in £?

feedback.correct: The impact rate rises by $\sqrt 2$ and the traded value doubles, so the cost rises by $2\sqrt 2$.
feedback.generic: Two things change. The impact per £ grows with the square root of size, and the value traded grows with size.

byKey.linear: You doubled the cost. Impact per £ also rises when the order does, so the cost grows faster than size.
byKey.old-notional: You raised the impact rate by $\sqrt 2$ but charged it on the old £2.4m. The order is now £4.8m.

explain.text: At 80,000 shares the rate is 0.015 × √0.05 = 0.335%, up from 0.237%. It applies to £4,800,000, so the cost is £16,099.69. That is 2.83 times the smaller order.

items.title: A month late
items.prose: A signal's monthly rank IC has mean 0.036 and sd 0.081 over 36 months that do not overlap. Its lagged IC has a half-life of two months. The desk can trade it only one month after it is formed.
items.question: Over 36 months, what t statistic should the late book's mean IC expect, with the same sd?

feedback.correct: One month is half a half-life, so the IC keeps $0.5^{1/2} = 0.707$ of itself.
feedback.generic: Decay the IC by the delay first. Then divide by its standard error, the sd over $\sqrt n$.

byKey.no-delay: You used the IC as it is formed. One month late, it has decayed.
byKey.halved: You halved the IC. A two-month half-life halves it over two months, not one.
byKey.ir: You divided the IC by the sd. The t statistic needs $\sqrt{36}$ as well.

explain.text: One month late the IC is $0.036 \times 0.5^{1/2} = 0.0255$. Its standard error is $0.081/\sqrt{36} = 0.0135$. The t statistic is 1.89, below 2, so the late book's edge is no longer clear.

items.title: Three pricers on one grid
items.prose:
Six-month puts on a £100 share, $r = 5\%$, $q = 1\%$, $\sigma = 20\%$. EU and US are 500-step European and American trees. MC is 100,000 antithetic paths, with standard error se. A pricer error is one of three things:

- a European tree more than £0.01 from Black-Scholes
- a Monte Carlo price more than 3 standard errors away
- an American tree below the European tree, or below the exercise value $K - S$
items.question: Tap every cell that signals a pricer error.

feedback.correct: Four cells break a rule: the European tree at 110, Monte Carlo at 90, and the American tree at 100 and 120.
feedback.generic: Test each column against its rule. An American put may be worth more than a European one, but never less than $K - S$.

byKey.premium: You flagged the American premium at 110. Early exercise adds value to a deep in-the-money put, so it is expected.
byKey.r3c2: The European tree at 110 is £0.12 from Black-Scholes, and the limit is £0.01.
byKey.r1c3: At 90 the Monte Carlo price is 3.7 standard errors below Black-Scholes. The limit is 3.
byKey.r2c5: At 100 the American tree is £0.10 below the European tree. An American option is never worth less.
byKey.r3c3: That Monte Carlo price is 1.8 standard errors from Black-Scholes. Inside 3 is noise.
byKey.r3c5: Early exercise adds value to a put this far in the money. A premium over the European tree is expected.
byKey.r4c5: At 120 the American put is £19.95, below the £20.00 it pays if exercised now. That is a pricer error.

explain.text: The European tree misses at 110, Monte Carlo misses at 90, and the American tree sits below the European at 100. At 120 it is below the £20.00 that exercise pays today. The premium at 110 is early exercise, not error.

items.title: Lines that peek
items.prose: A colleague's engine decides at each close and fills at the next open. These lines build its inputs from daily data, where `close` is a pandas Series and `ret` its daily returns.
items.question: Which lines use information from the future? Select all that apply.

options.text: `m = close.resample('ME').last().pct_change().reindex(close.index, method='bfill')`, the month's return on each of its days
`pct = ret.rank(pct=True)`, each day's return ranked against the whole sample

options.why: Forward filling carries the last known price forward. It uses only the past.
An exponential average weights past returns only. Nothing here reads a later bar.
The five-day return looks backwards, and `shift(1)` delays it by a bar. Nothing here uses a later bar.

feedback.correct: A month-end value copied back, an interpolated gap and a whole-sample rank all read later bars.
feedback.generic: Ask of each line: could it be computed at that bar's close, with nothing later in the file?

byKey.ffill: You flagged forward filling. It copies yesterday's price into a gap, so it looks only back.
byKey.lag: You flagged the shifted return. It looks back five bars and then waits a bar more.
byKey.ewm: You flagged the exponential sd. It weights only returns already seen.

explain.text: A month's return is known only at month end, so copying it back peeks. `interpolate` draws a line to the next known price, and a whole-sample rank compares today with later days. `ffill`, an exponential sd and a lagged return use only the past.

items.title: A rank IC by hand
items.prose: Seven shares at the end of a month. S7 has no signal today, so it stays out. The rank IC is the correlation between the ranks of the signal and the ranks of next month's return.
items.question: What is the rank IC? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.correct: S1 and S6 share rank 4.5. The correlation of the two rank lists is 0.667.
feedback.generic: Rank the six signals, giving tied values the average rank. Then correlate the two rank lists.

byKey.formula: You used $1 - 6\sum d^2/(n(n^2-1))$. With a tie it is only close, so correlate the ranks themselves.
byKey.pearson: You correlated the raw values. The 6.0% return pulls that up. A rank IC uses ranks only.

explain.text: Signal ranks are 4.5, 2, 6, 3, 1, 4.5 and return ranks are 2, 3, 6, 5, 1, 4. Both have mean 3.5; the cross products sum to 11.5 and the squares to 17 and 17.5. The IC is $11.5/\sqrt{17 \times 17.5} = 0.667$, where the no-ties formula gives 0.671.

items.title: Spot vols from forward vols
items.prose: Total variance adds over time: $w(T) = \sum_i \sigma_{f,i}^2\,\Delta T_i$, where $\sigma_{f,i}$ is the forward vol over the $i$-th interval. The vol to expiry $T$ is $\sqrt{w(T)/T}$. A desk quotes forward vols for 0 to $T_1$, $T_1$ to $T_2$, and so on.
items.question: Write `term_vols(expiries, fwd_vols)`. Return the vol to each expiry. Raise `ValueError` if the lists differ in length, the expiries are not positive and strictly increasing, or a forward vol is negative.

widget.starter:
import math

def term_vols(expiries, fwd_vols):
    """Vol to each expiry from the forward vols of the intervals before it."""
    out, w, prev = [], 0.0, 0.0
    for T, f in zip(expiries, fwd_vols):
        # add this interval's variance to the total
        ...
        # the vol to T from the total variance
        ...
    return out
widget.how: Submit runs 11 hidden tests. They cover rising and falling forward vols, a flat curve, a zero forward vol, one expiry, empty lists and bad inputs. Floats are compared within 2e-6.

feedback.correct: Each forward variance is added over its own interval, and the total is divided by the expiry.
feedback.generic: Add $\sigma_f^2\,\Delta T$ interval by interval. Then take $\sqrt{w/T}$, never an average of vols.

explain.text: Variance, not volatility, adds over time, so each interval adds its forward variance times its length. The vol to an expiry is the root of that total over the time. Averaging the forward vols would ignore how long each one lasts.

items.title: Reading a drawdown and a Calmar ratio
items.prose: Month-end equity of a strategy, in £k, over a year: `100 104 109 103 98 101 107 112 108 115 119 121 118.4`. Measure drawdown on these points.
items.question: Fill in the four measures.

rows: Maximum drawdown (%, as a positive number)
Longest spell below the running peak (months)

feedback.correct: The worst fall is 109 to 98, it lasts four months, and Calmar is about 1.82.
feedback.generic: Track the running peak. Drawdown is the value over the peak so far, minus 1, at its worst point.

byKey.global-range: Measure each fall from the peak so far, not from the highest to the lowest point overall.
byKey.global-calmar: You divided by the highest-to-lowest range, not the largest fall from a running peak.
byKey.r3c1: Calmar is the yearly growth over the size of the maximum drawdown.
byKey.with-recovery: You counted the month equity regained the peak. The spell is the months below it: 103, 98, 101 and 107.

explain.text: The worst fall is 109 to 98, 11 over 109 or 10.09%, and equity stays below 109 for four months. The year grows 18.4%, so Calmar is 18.4 / 10.09 = 1.82. Using 121 and 98 would give 19.0%, comparing a trough with a later peak.

items.title: Rank weights for a long-short book
items.prose: Eight shares, one signal each. Build dollar-neutral rank weights: centre the ranks on their mean, then scale so the absolute weights sum to 1. S6 has no signal today.
items.question: Fill in the missing weights, as decimals.

feedback.correct: S4 and S7 share rank 4.5. Centred ranks run from −3 to 3 and sum to 12 in size.
feedback.generic: Rank the seven shares with a signal, giving tied values the average rank. Centre on the mean rank, 4, then divide by the sum of sizes.

byKey.r5c2: S6 has no signal, so it is not ranked. Its weight is zero, and the other seven are ranked among themselves.
byKey.r3c2: S4 ties with S7 at 0.5. Each takes rank 4.5, a centred rank of 0.5, so 0.5 / 12.
byKey.r0c2: S1 ranks sixth of seven, a centred rank of 2. Divide by 12.
byKey.r2c2: S3 ranks first of seven, a centred rank of 3. Divide by 12.
byKey.r7c2: S8 ranks second from the bottom, a centred rank of −2. Divide by 12.
byKey.tie-order: You broke the tie by order. S4 and S7 share ranks 4 and 5, so each takes 4.5.

explain.text: From the bottom: S5, S8 and S2, then S4 and S7 tied at 4.5, then S1 and S3. Centred ranks are −3, −2, −1, 0.5, 0.5, 2 and 3, which sum to 12 in size. S4 gets 0.5 / 12 = 0.0417 and S3 gets 3 / 12 = 0.25.

items.title: Explaining a day's P&L
items.prose: One six-month at-the-money put. The pricer gives delta −0.4023, gamma 0.0274, vega 27.36 per 1.00 of volatility and theta −3.24 a year. Over one day the share falls £3, volatility rises 2 points and a day passes. Full repricing shows the put up £1.8706.
items.question: Fill in the Greek terms, their total and the residual, in £.

feedback.correct: The Greeks explain £1.8685 of the £1.8706 move. The residual is £0.0021.
feedback.generic: Delta times the move. Half gamma times the move squared. Vega times the change in vol. Theta times the fraction of a year.

byKey.no-half: The gamma term is $\tfrac12 \Gamma\,dS^2$. You may have left out the half.
byKey.r5c1: The residual is the actual change minus the explained total.
byKey.delta-sign: Delta is negative and so is the move, so the delta term is positive.
byKey.vega-units: This vega is per 1.00 of volatility. Two points is 0.02, so the term is 0.5472.
byKey.theta-year: Theta here is per year. One day is a 365th of it.

explain.text: Delta gives −0.4023 × −3 = 1.2069 and gamma 0.5 × 0.0274 × 9 = 0.1233. Vega gives 27.36 × 0.02 = 0.5472 and theta −3.24 / 365 = −0.0089. The total is 1.8685, so the residual against 1.8706 is 0.0021.

items.title: One line of a tear sheet
items.prose:
A backtest gives daily equity and the weight held each day, as a fraction of equity. The conventions are the course's.

- Sharpe: $\sqrt{\text{periods}}$ times the mean over the sample sd (ddof 1) of simple returns. It is 0.0 for fewer than two returns or no spread.
- Maximum drawdown: the worst fall from a running peak, a fraction of at most 0.
- CAGR: $(E_{\text{last}} / E_{\text{first}})^{\text{periods}/(n-1)} - 1$ for $n$ values.
- Calmar: CAGR over the size of the maximum drawdown, or `math.inf` with no drawdown.
- Turnover: the mean absolute daily change in weight over all $n$ days, with weight 0 before day 1.
items.question: Write `tear_line(equity, weights, periods=252)` returning `(sharpe, max_drawdown, calmar, turnover)`.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def tear_line(equity, weights, periods=252):
    """(sharpe, max_drawdown, calmar, turnover) of one backtest."""
    r = equity.pct_change().dropna()
    # sqrt(periods) * mean / sample sd; 0.0 if undefined
    sharpe = ...
    # worst fall from a running peak, a fraction <= 0
    max_dd = ...
    # growth per year from the first to the last value
    cagr = ...
    # cagr / |max_dd|; inf when there is no drawdown
    calmar = ...
    # mean |change in weight| per day, starting from 0
    turnover = ...
    return sharpe, max_dd, calmar, turnover
widget.solution:
import math
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def tear_line(equity, weights, periods=252):
    """(sharpe, max_drawdown, calmar, turnover) of one backtest."""
    eq = pd.Series(equity, dtype=float)
    r = eq.pct_change().dropna()
    sd = r.std(ddof=1) if len(r) > 1 else 0.0
    sharpe = 0.0 if not sd > 1e-12 else float(np.sqrt(periods) * r.mean() / sd)
    max_dd = float((eq / eq.cummax() - 1).min())
    cagr = float((eq.iloc[-1] / eq.iloc[0]) ** (periods / (len(eq) - 1)) - 1)
    calmar = cagr / abs(max_dd) if max_dd < 0 else math.inf
    w = np.asarray(weights, dtype=float)
    turnover = float(np.abs(np.diff(w, prepend=0.0)).mean())
    return sharpe, max_dd, calmar, turnover

examples.call: [round(v, 6) for v in tear_line(e, w, periods=12)]

tests.call: [round(v, 6) for v in tear_line(e, w, periods=12)]
[round(v, 6) for i, v in enumerate(tear_line(e, w)) if i != 2]
[round(v, 6) for v in tear_line(e, w, periods=252)]

rng = np.random.default_rng(11); e = pd.Series(1e6 * np.cumprod(1 + rng.normal(-0.0002, 0.012, 400))); w = pd.Series(np.round(rng.uniform(-1, 1, 400), 2))

widget.how: Submit runs 7 hidden tests. They cover a monthly series, a rising curve, a flat curve, a short series and two seeded series. Floats are compared within 2e-6. The first run loads NumPy and pandas, 10 to 30 seconds.
widget.prelude:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

feedback.correct: All four numbers follow the course's conventions, including the edge cases.
feedback.generic: Check each convention in turn. The Sharpe uses ddof 1. The drawdown uses a running peak. The CAGR exponent is periods over n − 1.

explain.text: Each number has one convention that is easy to miss. The Sharpe uses the sample sd, the drawdown a running peak, and the CAGR n − 1 returns. A curve that never falls has no drawdown, so its Calmar is infinite.

items.title: What costs leave of a book

import numpy as np

def leak_rows(run, bars, cut):
    """Rows before cut whose value changes when the bars after cut
    are replaced by noise."""
    full = run(bars).iloc[:cut].to_numpy(float)
    noisy = run(noise_after(bars, cut)).iloc[:cut].to_numpy(float)
    diff = ~np.isclose(full, noisy, rtol=0, atol=1e-9, equal_nan=True)
    return [int(i) for i in np.flatnonzero(diff)]

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def sector_zscore(signal, sector, min_names=3):
    """z-score each share against its own sector, date by date."""
    out = pd.DataFrame(np.nan, index=signal.index, columns=signal.columns)
    for name in sector.unique():
        cols = list(sector.index[sector == name])
        block = signal[cols]
        n = block.notna().sum(axis=1)
        mu = block.mean(axis=1)
        sd = block.std(axis=1, ddof=1)
        z = block.sub(mu, axis=0).div(sd, axis=0)
        ok = (n >= min_names) & (sd > 1e-12)
        out[cols] = z.where(ok, np.nan, axis=0)
    return out

items.title: A bumped gamma of zero
items.prose: Gamma by a central bump is $(V(S+h) - 2V(S) + V(S-h))/h^2$. A colleague runs it on a three-month call. From the last row they report 'zero gamma'.
items.question: From the $h = 1$ row, the truncation error is about $6.4 \times 10^{-5}\,h^2$. Round-off is about $\varepsilon V/h^2$, with $\varepsilon V = 1.5 \times 10^{-16}$ for this £1.35 call. At what $h$ are the two equal? Give 2 significant figures.

feedback.generic: Set $c\,h^2 = \varepsilon V/h^2$ and solve for $h$.

byKey.square-root: You took a square root. Both errors carry $h^2$, so $h^4$ is the ratio: take a fourth root.

items.title: A put with a few exercise dates
items.prose:
A Bermudan put can be exercised only on certain dates. On a CRR tree it may be exercised at step $i$ only if $i$ is in `exercise_steps`. Step 0 is today and step $n$ is expiry, where the put always pays $\max(K - S, 0)$. At an allowed step the holder takes the larger of the hold value and $K - S_{ij}$.

The starter builds the tree and the hold values. The tree uses $u = e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}$, $d = 1/u$ and $p = (e^{(r-q)\Delta t} - d)/(u - d)$.
items.question: Write the exercise step so that `bermudan_put` returns the right price.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np

def bermudan_put(S, K, r, sigma, T, n, exercise_steps, q=0.0):
    """CRR tree price of a put that may be exercised only at the
    given steps (0 is today, n is expiry; expiry always pays)."""
    dt = T / n
    u = np.exp(sigma * np.sqrt(dt))
    d = 1 / u
    p = (np.exp((r - q) * dt) - d) / (u - d)
    disc = np.exp(-r * dt)
    j = np.arange(n + 1)
    # payoffs at step n
    V = np.maximum(K - S * u ** (2 * j - n), 0.0)
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        # hold value at step i
        V = disc * (p * V[1:] + (1 - p) * V[:-1])
        # exercise here only if i is an allowed step
        ...
    return float(V[0])
widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def bermudan_put(S, K, r, sigma, T, n, exercise_steps, q=0.0):
    """CRR tree price of a put that may be exercised only at the
    given steps (0 is today, n is expiry; expiry always pays)."""
    dt = T / n
    u = np.exp(sigma * np.sqrt(dt))
    d = 1 / u
    p = (np.exp((r - q) * dt) - d) / (u - d)
    disc = np.exp(-r * dt)
    allowed = set(int(s) for s in exercise_steps)
    j = np.arange(n + 1)
    V = np.maximum(K - S * u ** (2 * j - n), 0.0)      # payoffs at step n
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        V = disc * (p * V[1:] + (1 - p) * V[:-1])      # hold value at step i
        if i in allowed:
            nodes = S * u ** (2 * np.arange(i + 1) - i)
            V = np.maximum(V, K - nodes)               # exercise value
    return float(V[0])

explain.text: The backward loop already gives the hold value at each step. At an allowed step we replace it by the larger of hold and exercise, node by node. With no allowed step the price is European, and with every step allowed it is American.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def net_book(signal, ret, half_spread_bp, every=5, min_names=4):
    """Daily gross and net returns of a rank-weighted long-short book."""
    n = len(signal)
    k = signal.shape[1]
    weights = np.zeros((n, k))                # the book held over each row
    cost = np.zeros(n)                        # cost charged on each row
    w_prev = np.zeros(k)
    reb = list(range(every - 1, n, every))
    for j, p in enumerate(reb):
        s = signal.iloc[p]
        valid = s.notna().to_numpy()
        w = np.zeros(k)
        if valid.sum() >= min_names:
            r = s.rank().to_numpy()
            d = np.where(valid, r - np.nanmean(r), 0.0)
            gross = np.abs(d).sum()
            if gross > 0:
                w = d / gross
        stop = reb[j + 1] if j + 1 < len(reb) else n - 1
        weights[p + 1:stop + 1] = w
        if p + 1 < n:
            cost[p + 1] = half_spread_bp / 1e4 * np.abs(w - w_prev).sum()
        w_prev = w
    r = np.nan_to_num(ret.to_numpy(float))
    gross = (weights * r).sum(axis=1)
    out = pd.DataFrame({"gross": gross, "net": gross - cost}, index=signal.index)
    return out.iloc[reb[0] + 1:] if reb else out.iloc[0:0]

items.title: Reviewing a results note
items.prompt:
A colleague sends a results note for a five-day momentum rule on one share. It uses five years of daily bars. Its claims:

- Net Sharpe 2.4 after 2 bp a trade.
- 60 lookback and threshold settings were tried, and the best is reported. The 60 Sharpes had mean 0.5 and sd 0.7.
- Orders fill at the close of the signal bar.
- The held-out year was opened twice while tuning. Its Sharpe was 0.3, so it was averaged with the research period.
- What failed: nothing.

Write your review.

(a) Name the problems in the order you would check them, and say why that order.

(b) For two of them, give a number or a test that shows how large the problem is.

(c) Rewrite the "What failed" section so that it is honest.
items.model:
**(a) Problems, in order.**

1. *A Sharpe of 2.4 on a simple rule is a bug until proved otherwise.* I check it first. Every other number depends on the engine. I run the look-ahead test. I cut the bars at several rows and replace everything after each cut with noise. No earlier row may change.
2. *The fill.* Orders fill at the close of the signal bar, a price the rule has just seen. That is the same-bar rule, and it manufactures edge. The fix is a fill at the next open, with costs and slippage that grow with size.
3. *Selection.* The note reports the best of 60 settings. If no setting were better than the others, the best of 60 would be expected near $0.5 + 0.7 \times 2.32 = 2.12$. The reported 2.4 is only 0.4 of their sd above that, so chance can give it.
4. *The held-out year.* It was opened twice, so it is no longer held out. Averaging it with the research period mixes a spent number into a clean one. A year of daily data has a Sharpe standard error near 1.0. So 0.3 neither confirms nor rejects the rule. Report it alone, as a single look.
5. *Costs.* 2 bp ignores commission and the impact of size. I would ask for turnover and a full cost bill.

**(b) Numbers.** A daily rule with equal-sized wins and losses needs about 57.5% winning days to reach 2.4. That solves $\sqrt{252}\,(2p-1)/\sqrt{1-(2p-1)^2} = 2.4$ for $p = 0.575$. Real daily bars rarely allow that, which supports the bug reading. For selection, the expected best of 60 equal settings is about 2.12, against the reported 2.4. I would also ask for the count and spread of all 60 results.

**(c) What failed.**

"The first version filled at the close of the signal bar and reached a Sharpe of 2.4. We need a look-ahead test and next-open fills before quoting any figure. We tried 60 settings, with Sharpes of mean 0.5 and sd 0.7. The best of them is about what the best of 60 equal settings would give. The held-out year was opened twice during tuning, so it is no longer clean. Its Sharpe of 0.3 has a standard error near 1.0 and supports no conclusion. We do not claim an edge."

rubric.text: Treats a Sharpe of 2.4 on a simple rule as a bug first. Proposes the look-ahead test: cut, add noise after the cut, compare earlier rows.
Spots the fill at the signal bar's close as a same-bar fill. Moves it to the next open with realistic costs.
Spots the selection problem: among equal settings, the best of 60 is near what chance gives, about 2.1. Asks for the count and spread, or a deflated comparison.
Says the twice-opened held-out year is spent. Rejects averaging it in. Notes its Sharpe of 0.3 has a standard error near 1.
Sizes a problem with a number or test: the 57.5% hit rate, the expected maximum, or the standard error.
Writes a specific "What failed" paragraph: the bug, the 60 settings, the held-out year. Not "nothing".

explain.text: Check the engine before the statistics, then the selection, then the held-out data. A note that reports only what worked has not said what failed.
